sections.overview: Ailurus fulgens is the western, Himalayan red panda, a small carnivoran in the family Ailuridae. Mammal taxonomies now commonly list it separately from the Chinese red panda, A. styani, although the species rank of these lineages remains debated.
sections.identification: Look for a rusty-red back, dark underside, pale face with reddish tear marks, pointed ears and a thick ringed tail. Fur covers the feet; five toes bear semi-retractile claws, and an enlarged wrist bone forms a gripping pseudo-thumb. The Smithsonian reports adults at 56–62.5 cm in body length plus a 37–47.2 cm tail, weighing 3.6–7.7 kg. The sources give no standard body height or width, nor separate adult dimensions for males and females. Compared with A. styani, A. fulgens tends to have a paler, more white-marked face and less distinct tail rings.
sections.habitat: It occupies cool, temperate mountain forests with bamboo in the understory, in the eastern Himalaya and adjoining highlands. Field studies record it mainly at roughly 2,100–4,325 m; the exact elevations and forest structure used vary across the range.
sections.diet: Bamboo leaves and young shoots dominate its food, although estimates vary among studies and sites. It selects nutritious parts and may supplement them with roots, grasses, fruit, insects, eggs and small vertebrates.
sections.behavior: Field accounts from Nepal describe solitary animals outside the breeding season, most active in the early morning and evening, and resting in branches or tree hollows during the day.
sections.reproduction: In the Northern Hemisphere, mating usually occurs from January to March. Delayed implantation makes the interval to birth variable, roughly 93–156 days; females den in cavities or dense cover and typically raise two furred cubs, which remain with their mother for about a year.
sections.ecology: This is a bamboo and cool-forest specialist: surveys in Nepal found bamboo abundance to be a consistent predictor of its occurrence, with water, canopy and other forest features also mattering by region. Because bamboo is relatively low in energy, the animal spends much of its active time feeding and selects tender leaves and shoots.
sections.conservation: The Mammal Diversity Database lists A. fulgens as Endangered. Habitat loss and fragmentation threaten this forest specialist. Other documented pressures include livestock competition, habitat degradation, poaching and disease transmitted by dogs.
